title: Our Commitment | Grambling State University
text: Our Commitment A campus where everybody is somebody Grambling State University is committed to fostering a campus culture defined by leadership, mutual respect, and student success. Eliminating hazing is essential to that promise. What We Stand For Our commitment to ending hazing Eliminating hazing is essential to strengthening our culture and ensuring the safety and dignity of every member of our community. Hazing is a crime under Louisiana law and a direct violation of University policy. Grambling State University strictly prohibits hazing in any form, against any individual, organization, or member of the campus community. This site provides clear guidance on what GSU stands for: belonging, accountability, and care for one another, as well as what behaviors we do not tolerate. Here, you will find education, prevention tools, reporting pathways, and support resources designed to keep our community informed and empowered. If you have a concern or need to report an incident, please visit the Report It page. Our Values The principles that guide us Belonging Every student deserves a place to grow and lead. Real community is built on respect, never on harm. Accountability We hold organizations and individuals to clear standards, and we report confirmed violations transparently. Care for one another We look out for each other. Support, recovery, and education are central to how we keep students safe. The People Behind Prevention The Hazing Prevention Team A multidisciplinary team of educators, staff, and faculty leads our prevention work year-round, providing education, support, expectations, and accountability across campus. Meet the Team Our Promise To be a place where everybody is somebody. Thank you for helping Grambling State University uphold our enduring promise. Report a concern, learn the signs, and stand with us. Report a Hazing Incident Learn About Hazing

title: Hazing Transparency Report | Grambling State University
text: Accountability & Transparency Hazing Transparency Report In accordance with the Stop Campus Hazing Act (SCHA), Grambling State University will maintain a Campus Hazing Transparency Report (CHTR). This report provides information on confirmed hazing violations by organizations formally recognized by the University. The CHTR will be updated biannually, as required. title: Parents & Family | Grambling State University
text: Parents & Family You're part of the prevention team It's important to speak with your student about hazing, because it can occur within any student group or organization. Consistent communication is one of the most powerful tools to prevent it. Start the Talk Start the conversation Speak respectfully Your student respects your judgment. A non-judgmental tone keeps the door open. Be persistent Move the conversation forward. Check in regularly, not just once. Understand the pull Belonging matters. Acknowledge the desire to fit in, and be there before harm happens. Report right away If you suspect hazing, make a report. You don't need proof to raise a concern. Questions to ask your student Are you in the process of joining an organization or team? How much time do you spend on new-member activities? Are you having trouble keeping up with academics? Are you being deprived of anything, such as sleep? What would you tell me about a hazing incident? Do you feel safe and respected in your organization? Trust Your Instincts Warning signs to watch for No single sign means hazing is happening, but several together are worth a closer conversation. Sudden secrecy Your student stops sharing details about meetings or activities. Unexplained injuries Bruises, exhaustion, or changes in how they look or move. Becoming isolated Pulling away from family, friends, or their usual support. Mood or sleep changes New anxiety, irritability, or disrupted sleeping and eating habits. Drop in grades Activities consuming all their time and hurting coursework. Odd hours & errands Always being asked to run errands or perform tasks at all hours. You're Not Alone How GSU supports your student Confidential care, advising, and recovery resources A team of Student Affairs staff ready to help Anonymous reporting through the G Safe app Transparent reporting that holds organizations accountable Contact Student Affairs Worried about your student? Reach out. You can make a report anonymously, or talk it through with the Dean of Students office. Report a Concern

title: How to Prevent | Grambling State University
text: Prevention & Education How to Prevent The fight against hazing is everyone's responsibility. These tips help students and community members know how to recognize, respond to, and proactively prevent hazing. Speak Up The first step to ending hazing is to identify it and make your voice heard. Ask specific, clarifying questions if you see something that could be considered hazing. Questions you can ask “I noticed you missed last night's meeting. You look tired and in pain—is everything ok?” “I saw you wearing a funny outfit in class today. Did someone force you to wear that?” “You haven't turned in your homework and your grades dropped. What's going on?” “Why do you have so many bruises on you? Did someone hit you?” “How did that symbol appear on your skin? Were you branded?” “We haven't seen you in a few weeks. Are you being forced to self-isolate?” Remember, these conversations are always situational and contextual. You're more likely to get an honest response if the person trusts you. Even if they insist they aren't being hazed, hazing occurs with and without the victim's consent. Hazing Prevention Training Complete the free online Vector Solutions LMS training for hazing prevention. The full course is approximately 27 minutes long. title: Hazing FAQ | Grambling State University
text: Understanding Hazing Frequently Asked Questions Clear answers to common questions about hazing, the law, and how to report a concern. What is hazing? Hazing is when a person intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly causes, coerces, or forces another individual to engage in or endure certain actions for the purpose of pre-initiation activities, pledging, initiating, holding office, admitting, or affiliating into or with an organization, or for the purpose of continuing, reinstating, or enhancing an individual's membership or status in an organization. For a fuller description, visit the What Is Hazing page. Is hazing illegal? Yes. Hazing is considered a crime. Can I get sued for hazing? Yes. In addition to criminal penalties and University sanctions, an individual who engages in hazing could be sued and forced to pay significant monetary damages (along with attorney's fees) as part of a civil suit. These suits have resulted in judgements totaling millions of dollars. Isn't hazing ok if no one gets hurt? No. Any form of hazing, regardless of the outcome, is a crime in Louisiana and a violation of University policy. It does not become ok, legal, or permissible if no harm is intended or occurs. Verbal and emotional abuse can be just as damaging as physical abuse. Have people died from hazing? Sadly, yes. There are deaths attributable to hazing at other schools every year. In each of those situations, the individuals who engaged in the hazing probably thought what they were doing was harmless and would not result in someone's death. My group has always hazed new members. Isn't it a tradition? No. "Tradition" does not justify committing a crime or violating University policy. Traditions are created by groups, and groups hold the power to change or eliminate them. It only takes one year to break a hazing tradition. Remember that the founding members of organizations were not hazed. Our new members voluntarily participate, so that can't be hazing, right? Wrong. Under Louisiana state law and GSU policy, the fact that a person consented to a hazing activity is not a defense. The peer pressure and desire to belong in a student organization can create a coercive environment where true consent cannot be given. In short, an individual cannot consent to being hazed. Doesn't hazing teach respect and make better members? No. Respect is earned, not demanded or taught. When respect is earned, there is also trust. Hazing only motivates people out of fear and anxiety. Doesn't hazing help build a bond among new members? No. Hazing isolates each member from the established group. It does not promote organizational unity. There are safer and more productive ways to build friendships and community. Do I have a duty to report hazing? Yes. All members of the campus community have an obligation to promptly report any good-faith concerns about hazing that has occurred or will occur. If I know about hazing but don't promptly report it, what happens to me? If you are a student, you may be subject to charges and sanctions under the Code of Student Conduct. Employees may be subject to discipline. How do I report concerns about hazing? If the situation is an emergency and you or someone else needs immediate assistance, call 911 or contact GSUPD at 318-274-2222 . For non-emergency situations, see our reporting options . Any report should include as much detail as possible (who, where, when, and what happened). Still have a concern? You don't have to be certain. If something feels wrong, report it and we will take it from there. Report a Concern What Is Hazing?

title: What Is Hazing? | Grambling State University
text: Know It When You See It What Is Hazing? Hazing takes many forms and can be tricky to identify. It often hides behind tradition, secrecy, and the idea of "earning" your place. Learn the signs so you'll recognize it. Hazing is any activity expected of someone joining or participating in a group that humiliates, degrades, abuses, or endangers them, regardless of their willingness to participate. GSU Code of Student Conduct & StopHazing.org Understanding Severity The Spectrum of Hazing, it's all hazing Hazing exists on a spectrum, from subtle to severe. Behaviors at the "milder" end are easy to excuse, but they are exactly what escalate over time. Every level is still hazing. Intimidation Lower Severity Lies and purposeful deception Assigning demerits or punishment Forced silence Social isolation of new members Use of demeaning names Expecting members to carry certain items at all times Harassment Moderate Severity Verbal abuse Threats or implied threats Asking members to wear humiliating clothing Forced servitude "Skit nights" with humiliating acts Sleep deprivation Requiring new members to learn songs or chants Violence High Severity Forced or coerced use of food, alcohol, or other drugs Beating, paddling, or any form of physical assault Branding Staged kidnappings Sexual assault Forced consumption of vile substances All of This Is Hazing Examples of hazing Drawn directly from the GSU Code of Student Conduct. These actions qualify as hazing regardless of a person's willingness to participate. Substances & alcohol Forced or coerced consumption of food, alcohol, drugs, or any other substance Placement of undesirable substances on or in the body Deprivation of food or water Physical strain Unnecessary physical contact such as whipping, beating, paddling, or branding Calisthenics such as sit-ups, push-ups, or wall sits Unnecessary fatigue, physical activity, or sleep deprivation Control & servitude Servitude for personal benefit such as driving, cooking, cleaning, or running errands Required periods of silence or forced wearing of inappropriate apparel Lineups or events where individuals are yelled or cursed at Policy & Law The rules that prohibit hazing Hazing is a crime under Louisiana law and a direct violation of University policy. title: State Law | Grambling State University
text: Understanding Hazing State Law Louisiana has a statewide, zero-tolerance approach to hazing, with anti-hazing laws and uniform policy guidance for Louisiana institutions. Louisiana Anti-Hazing Law How the law defines hazing Under Louisiana law, hazing is an intentional, knowing, or reckless act directed against another person when both of the following apply: The person knew or should have known that the act endangers the physical health or safety of the other person or causes severe emotional distress. The act was associated with pledging, being initiated into, affiliating with, participating in, holding office in, or maintaining membership in any organization. Hazing includes physical brutality, dangerous physical activity, forced consumption of food or substances (including alcohol or drugs), and activity that requires someone to commit a crime or another act of hazing. Normal, customary athletic or military training activities sanctioned by the institution are not considered hazing. At publicly funded Louisiana institutions, hazing in any form is prohibited. Organizations must report hazing incidents to their institution, and institutions must report alleged hazing to law enforcement without redacting names or details. Legislation Anti-hazing legislation The Louisiana Board of Regents maintains a current overview of Louisiana's anti-hazing legislation, including: Act 382 View PDF Act 635 View PDF Act 637 View PDF Act 640 View PDF Louisiana Anti-Hazing Laws & Resources Penalty Criminal hazing under La. R.S. 14:40.8 may be punished by fines, imprisonment, or both, with enhanced penalties when hazing causes serious bodily injury or death. Organizations and institutions may also face fines, loss of public funds, and loss of recognition. Students who violate La. R.S. 17:1801 may be expelled, suspended, or dismissed for at least one academic period. Credits: Acts 2018, No. 635, Secs. 1 and 2; Acts 2018, No. 640, Sec. 1; Acts 2019, No. 382, Secs. 1 and 2. Louisiana Revised Statutes 14:40.8 and 17:1801. Hazing is a crime. Report it. Reports can be made anonymously through the G Safe app or by calling GSUPD. Report a Concern What Is Hazing?
